solution.concept: BODMAS: both divisions and the multiplication come before the addition and subtraction
solution.explanation: Do the divisions and the multiplication first: 156 ÷ 12 = 13, 7 × 8 = 56 and 45 ÷ 9 = 5. Then 13 + 56 − 5 = 64.
solution.why_others_wrong: 74 adds the 5 instead of subtracting it; 155 adds 13 + 7 before multiplying by 8; 69 drops the last term.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the value of 0.25 × 4.8 + 2⅝ ÷ 0.75 − 1.6?

solution.concept: Convert mixed numbers and decimals to fractions; divide and multiply before adding and subtracting
solution.shortcut: Dividing by 0.75 is multiplying by 4/3: 2.625 × 4/3 = 3.5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.57 multiplies 2⅝ by 0.75 instead of dividing (1.2 + 1.97 − 1.6 ≈ 1.57); 6.3 adds the 1.6; 2.3 is 3.5 − 1.2, which drops the last term and subtracts the first.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the value of √5184 ÷ ∛1728 × √2.25 + 3².

solution.concept: Square roots and cube roots of perfect powers, then left-to-right ÷ and ×
solution.shortcut: 5184 ends in 4 and lies between 70² = 4900 and 75² = 5625, so its root is 72.
solution.why_others_wrong: 13 divides 6 by 1.5 instead of multiplying; 99 takes √2.25 as 15; 15 leaves out the × 1.5.

solution.concept: Negative fractional exponents: a^(−m/n) = 1 ÷ (n-th root of a)^m; write each decimal as a power of a simple fraction
solution.shortcut: A negative exponent flips the base: 0.2 → 5 and 0.5 → 2, then take the powers 5², 2³ and 2¹.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 divides by 4 instead of 2; 200 multiplies by 2 instead of dividing; 400 multiplies 25 × 8 × 2.

solution.concept: Open brackets from the innermost: ( ), then { }, then [ ]; division comes before subtraction
solution.why_others_wrong: 10.25 divides (45 − 4) by 4; 42.25 works out (15 − 8 + 3) × 2 = 20 inside the round bracket; 41 forgets the ÷ 4.

solution.concept: 'of' is worked out before division (the O in BODMAS)
solution.explanation: The bracket is 2⅖ + 3⅗ = 6. '⅗ of 15' = 9 is evaluated before the division, so 6 ÷ 9 = ⅔. Then ⅔ + 1⅓ = 2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 151⅓ divides by ⅗ first and then multiplies by 15, ignoring that 'of' comes first; 11⅓ drops the 'of 15'; ⅔ forgets to add 1⅓.

solution.concept: Square root of a decimal: the root has half as many decimal places
solution.explanation: √0.000441 = 0.021 (six decimal places become three), √0.0196 = 0.14 and √1.44 = 1.2. Multiplication first: 0.14 × 1.2 = 0.168. Then 0.021 + 0.168 = 0.189.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.378 takes √0.000441 as 0.21; 1.701 takes √0.0196 as 1.4; 0.1932 adds before multiplying.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If x = 3 + 2√2, what is the value of x³ + 1/x³?

solution.concept: Rationalising 1/x, then the identity a³ + b³ = (a + b)³ − 3ab(a + b) with ab = 1
solution.shortcut: Whenever x × (1/x) = 1, x³ + 1/x³ = k³ − 3k with k = x + 1/x.
solution.why_others_wrong: 216 is (x + 1/x)³ without the correction term; 234 adds 3(x + 1/x) instead of subtracting it; 34 is x² + 1/x² = 6² − 2, not the cube expression.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If 2^(x + 3) + 2^(x + 1) = 320, what is the value of x?

solution.concept: Take the lowest power out as a common factor
solution.explanation: 2^(x + 3) = 8 × 2^x and 2^(x + 1) = 2 × 2^x, so the left side is 10 × 2^x. Then 10 × 2^x = 320 gives 2^x = 32 = 2⁵, so x = 5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 is the value of x + 1 (factorising as 2^(x + 1)(2² + 1) = 320 gives 2^(x + 1) = 64), not of x; 4 and 3 fail the check: 2⁷ + 2⁵ = 160 and 2⁶ + 2⁴ = 80.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Express 0.2333… (3 recurring) + 0.363636… (36 recurring) as a fraction in its lowest terms.

solution.concept: Converting recurring decimals: pure recurring 0.abab… = ab/99; mixed recurring 0.abbb… = (ab − a)/90
solution.why_others_wrong: 59/99 treats both as pure recurring (23/99 + 36/99); 59/90 treats both as mixed with denominator 90; 19/30 writes 0.3636… as 36/90.

questions.question_text:

solution.concept: Evaluate every known term, then isolate ?²
solution.why_others_wrong: 30, 34 and 36 give ?² = 900, 1,156 and 1,296, none of which satisfies ?² + 6 = 1030.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the value of √(41 − √(21 + √(19 − √9))).

solution.concept: Nested radicals are opened from the innermost root outwards
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 is √25, the value one level inside, not the final root.

solution.concept: Rationalising: 1/(√a − √b) = (√a + √b)/(a − b), and here every a − b = 1
solution.explanation: Each term rationalises to a sum: 1/(√9 − √8) = 3 + √8, 1/(√8 − √7) = √8 + √7, and so on. With the alternating signs, (3 + √8) − (√8 + √7) + (√7 + √6) − (√6 + √5) + (√5 + 2) = 3 + 2 = 5, since all the surds cancel.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 assumes everything cancels, including 3 and 2; 1 subtracts 2 from 3; 3 + 2√2 keeps only the first term.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should replace ? in

solution.concept: Difference of squares a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b) after rounding
solution.shortcut: (a + b)(a − b) avoids squaring 17 and 13 separately.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the series?
11, 13, 16, 21, 28, 39, ?

solution.concept: Differences are consecutive prime numbers
solution.explanation: The differences are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, the prime numbers in order. The next prime is 13, so the next term is 39 + 13 = 52.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 repeats the difference 11; 51 uses 12, which is not prime.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the next term of the series: 120, 99, 80, 63, 48, ?

solution.concept: One less than perfect squares, in descending order
solution.shortcut: The differences 21, 19, 17, 15 fall by 2, so the next difference is 13: 48 − 13 = 35.
solution.why_others_wrong: 36 is 6² without the −1; 33 repeats the difference 15.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Which number should replace the question mark?
4, 10, 28, 82, 244, ?

solution.concept: Multiply by 3 and subtract 2
solution.explanation: Each term is three times the previous term minus 2: 4 × 3 − 2 = 10, 10 × 3 − 2 = 28, and so on. The next term is 244 × 3 − 2 = 730.
solution.shortcut: The differences 6, 18, 54, 162 triple, so the next difference is 486: 244 + 486 = 730.
solution.why_others_wrong: 732 multiplies by 3 without subtracting 2; 734 adds 2 instead.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the missing number (?) in the series: 64, 96, 144, ?, 324, 486

solution.concept: Each term is 1.5 times the previous term
solution.why_others_wrong: 192 repeats the difference 48; 240 adds 96. Neither continues to 324.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the missing term: 7, 8, 10, 14, 22, ?, 70

solution.concept: Differences double: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32
solution.explanation: The differences are 1, 2, 4, 8, so the next ones are 16 and 32. The missing term is 22 + 16 = 38, and 38 + 32 = 70 confirms it.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 repeats the difference 8; 46 doubles 22 and adds 2, but 46 → 70 is a difference of 24, not 32.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What will come in place of ? in the series 6, 24, 60, 120, 210, ?

solution.concept: n³ − n, i.e. the product of three consecutive numbers (n − 1) n (n + 1)
solution.why_others_wrong: 343 is 7³ without subtracting 7; 330 adds 120 (repeating a second difference of 30 instead of 36).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What should come in place of the question mark?
11, 25, 47, 97, 191, ?

solution.concept: Alternating operations: ×2 + 3, then ×2 − 3
solution.why_others_wrong: 379 applies −3 twice in a row; 382 doubles without the +3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the next term of the series: 3, 7, 13, 23, 41, 75, ?

solution.concept: Two levels of differences: the second differences double
solution.explanation: First differences: 4, 6, 10, 18, 34. Second differences: 2, 4, 8, 16, which double, so the next is 32. The next first difference is 34 + 32 = 66 and the next term is 75 + 66 = 141.
solution.shortcut: Each difference is twice the previous one minus 2 (6 = 2 × 4 − 2, 10 = 2 × 6 − 2, …): 2 × 34 − 2 = 66.
solution.why_others_wrong: 109 repeats the difference 34; 143 and 147 use second differences of 34 and 38.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
2, 12, 36, 80, 150, 252, ?

solution.concept: n² × (n + 1), which is n³ + n²
solution.shortcut: Check with differences: 10, 24, 44, 70, 102 → second differences 14, 20, 26, 32 → next 38 → 252 + 140 = 392.
solution.why_others_wrong: 343 is 7³ without the 7²; 384 uses a second difference of 30 instead of 38; 400 is 20².

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Which number will replace the question mark?
2, 5, 13, 36, 104, ?

solution.concept: Multiply by 3, then subtract 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
solution.why_others_wrong: 312 multiplies by 3 without subtracting; 308 repeats −4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the missing number: 5, 12, 10, 36, 20, 108, ?, 324

solution.concept: Two interleaved series
solution.explanation: The terms in odd positions are 5, 10, 20, ? (each doubled) and those in even positions are 12, 36, 108, 324 (each tripled). So the missing term is 20 × 2 = 40.
solution.why_others_wrong: 216 doubles 108 as if the series were one chain; 60 triples 20, mixing the two rules; 30 adds 10.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Which number in the series below does not fit the pattern?
7, 16, 35, 72, 153, 312, 631

solution.concept: Multiply by 2 and add 2, 3, 4, 5, …
solution.explanation: The rule is ×2 + 2, ×2 + 3, ×2 + 4, ×2 + 5, … The fourth term should be 35 × 2 + 4 = 74, and 74 × 2 + 5 = 153 confirms that 72 is wrong.
solution.why_others_wrong: 153 looks wrong if you continue from 72 (72 × 2 + 5 = 149), but it fits the correct value 74.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
1, 2, 6, 21, 88, 446, 2,676

solution.concept: Multiply by n and add n: ×1 + 1, ×2 + 2, ×3 + 3, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 2,676 looks wrong if you continue from 446 (446 × 6 + 6 = 2,682), but it fits 445.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Exactly one term of this series is incorrect. Which one?
4, 3, 5, 15, 55, 274, 1,643

solution.concept: Multiply by 1, 2, 3, … and subtract 1 each time
solution.why_others_wrong: 55 looks wrong if you continue from 15 (15 × 4 − 1 = 59), but it fits the correct value 14.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
In the following question, two equations I and II are given. Solve both and choose the correct relation between x and y.
I. x² − 15x + 56 = 0
II. y² − 3y − 10 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorising by splitting the middle term; a negative constant term gives roots of opposite signs
solution.explanation: x = 7 or 8. y = 5 or −2. The smallest x (7) is greater than the largest y (5), so x > y.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the roots of both equations below and state how x and y are related.
I. x² + 3x − 40 = 0
II. y² − 2y − 15 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Compare every pair of roots; a shared root plus opposite-side roots means no relation holds
solution.explanation: x = 5 or −8 and y = 5 or −3. x = −8 is smaller than both values of y, but x = 5 is greater than y = −3. So no single relation holds.
solution.why_others_wrong: x ≥ y and x ≤ y come from noticing the common root 5 and checking only one other pair.
solution.final_answer: Option B: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the roots of the following pair of equations and choose the relation between x and y that is always true.
I. 3x² − 19x + 30 = 0
II. 4y² − 25y + 36 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: When the root ranges overlap, no single relation holds
solution.explanation: x = 3 or 3.33 and y = 4 or 2.25. x is less than y = 4 but greater than y = 2.25, so no relation holds.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y comes from comparing only the larger roots (3.33 and 4).
solution.final_answer: Option C: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Work out every possible value of x and of y, then pick the relation that always holds.
I. x² = 289
II. y = √289

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: x² = k gives x = ±√k, but the symbol √k means only the positive root
solution.explanation: x² = 289 gives x = 17 or −17. y = √289 is the principal (positive) square root, so y = 17 only. x is either equal to y or smaller, so x ≤ y.
steps: II: y = +17 (the radical sign denotes the non-negative root)
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y misses the case x = y = 17; x ≥ y treats y = √289 as ±17 as well.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
One equation is linear and the other quadratic. Solve both and choose the correct relationship.
I. 4x − 7 = 2x + 9
II. y² − 17y + 72 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Solve the linear equation directly; factorise the quadratic
solution.explanation: I: 2x = 16, so x = 8. II: (y − 8)(y − 9) = 0, so y = 8 or 9. x is equal to or smaller than y, so x ≤ y.
steps: x = 8 = y (when y = 8) and x < y (when y = 9)
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y ignores y = 8.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
In the question below, solve equations I and II and identify the correct relation between x and y.
I. x² − (√3 + √2)x + √6 = 0
II. y² − 3√3y + 6 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Quadratics with surd coefficients: find two roots from their sum and product
solution.explanation: For I, the roots have sum √3 + √2 and product √6, so x = √3 or √2. For II, the roots have sum 3√3 and product 6, so y = √3 or 2√3. The largest x (√3) equals the smallest y (√3), so x ≤ y.
solution.shortcut: All roots are positive, so compare squares: x² ∈ {3, 2}, y² ∈ {3, 12}.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y misses the shared root √3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations and choose the option that correctly relates x and y.
I. 6x² + 13x + 6 = 0
II. 6y² + 5y − 6 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorising with a ≠ 1; check all four pairs
solution.explanation: x = −1.5 or −0.67 and y = −1.5 or 0.67. x = −0.67 is greater than y = −1.5 but less than y = 0.67, so no relation holds.
solution.why_others_wrong: x ≤ y comes from checking only x = −1.5 against both values of y.
solution.final_answer: Option B: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find all real values of x and y and choose the correct relation.
I. x³ − 512 = 0
II. y² − 15y + 56 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: A cube equation x³ = k has exactly one real root
solution.explanation: x³ = 512 has the single real root x = 8. y = 7 or 8. So x is greater than or equal to y: x ≥ y.
steps: I: x³ = 512 = 8³ ⇒ x = 8 (the only real root)
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y misses y = 8; x ≤ y comes from treating x³ = 512 like a square and adding x = −8.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations and choose the correct relation between x and y.
I. 2x² + 15x + 28 = 0
II. 5y² + 13y + 6 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: All coefficients positive ⇒ both roots negative; compare carefully on the negative side
solution.explanation: x = −3.5 or −4 and y = −0.6 or −2. The largest x (−3.5) is less than the smallest y (−2), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y comes from comparing the sizes 3.5, 4 with 0.6, 2 and forgetting the negative signs.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If the six-digit number 473x28 is divisible by 11, what is the digit x?

solution.concept: Divisibility by 11: (sum of digits in odd places) − (sum of digits in even places) must be 0 or a multiple of 11
solution.explanation: From the left, the odd places hold 4, 3, 2 (sum 9) and the even places hold 7, x, 8 (sum 15 + x). The difference 9 − (15 + x) = −(6 + x) must be a multiple of 11, so 6 + x = 11 and x = 5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6, 4 and 7 make the difference −12, −10 and −13, none of which is a multiple of 11.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two numbers are in the ratio 4 : 7 and their LCM is 1,092. What is the sum of the two numbers?

solution.concept: Numbers in ratio a : b (co-prime) are ak and bk with HCF k and LCM abk
solution.explanation: Let the numbers be 4k and 7k. Since 4 and 7 are co-prime, the LCM is 28k = 1,092, so k = 39. The numbers are 156 and 273, and their sum is 429.
solution.why_others_wrong: 273 is only the larger number; 546 is half the LCM, not the sum of the numbers; 390 would need k = 35, but 1,092 ÷ 28 = 39.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the remainder when 2¹⁰⁰ is divided by 7?

solution.concept: Find a power of the base that leaves remainder 1, then reduce the exponent
solution.explanation: 2³ = 8 leaves remainder 1 on division by 7. 2¹⁰⁰ = (2³)³³ × 2¹, so the remainder is 1³³ × 2 = 2.
solution.shortcut: Remainders of 2ⁿ ÷ 7 cycle 2, 4, 1; 100 leaves remainder 1 on division by 3, so take the first value, 2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 assumes 100 is a multiple of 3; 4 picks the second value of the cycle (as for an exponent ≡ 2 mod 3).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many zeros are there at the end of 250! (the product 1 × 2 × 3 × … × 250)?

solution.concept: Trailing zeros = number of factors 5 in n! (factors of 2 are always more): ⌊n/5⌋ + ⌊n/25⌋ + ⌊n/125⌋ + …
solution.explanation: Each trailing zero needs one factor 10 = 2 × 5, and 5s are scarcer than 2s. Multiples of 5 up to 250 give 50 fives, multiples of 25 give 10 extra, and multiples of 125 give 2 more. Total = 62.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 counts each multiple of 5 once; 60 stops at 25 and misses 125 and 250 (5³ factors); 52 skips the multiples of 25.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In an examination a candidate needs 40% of the maximum marks to pass. She scores 288 marks and fails by 12 marks. What are the maximum marks?

solution.concept: Pass marks = marks scored + shortfall = 40% of maximum
solution.explanation: The pass mark is 288 + 12 = 300. 300 is 40% of the maximum, so the maximum = 300 ÷ 0.4 = 750.
solution.why_others_wrong: 720 treats 288 as the pass mark; 690 subtracts 12 instead of adding it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The price of cooking oil rises by 25%. By what percentage must a household cut its consumption so that its spending on oil does not change?

solution.concept: Spending = price × consumption; reduction needed = r ÷ (100 + r) × 100
solution.explanation: If the price becomes 125/100 of the old price, consumption must become 100/125 = 4/5 of the old amount, a cut of 1/5 = 20%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25% simply copies the price rise; 16⅔% is the cut needed for a 20% price rise.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Rohit spends 72% of his monthly income and saves the rest. If he saves ₹7,840 a month, what is his monthly income?

solution.concept: Savings % = 100 − expenditure %
solution.explanation: He saves 100 − 72 = 28% of his income. 28% of income = ₹7,840, so income = 7,840 ÷ 0.28 = ₹28,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹20,160 is his expenditure (72% of ₹28,000); ₹10,889 divides 7,840 by 0.72.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A town has 50,000 people. Every year its population grows by a birth rate of 3.2% and falls by a death rate of 1.2% of the population at the start of that year (ignore migration). What will the population be after 2 years?

solution.concept: Net growth rate = birth rate − death rate, compounded yearly
solution.explanation: The net growth is 3.2% − 1.2% = 2% a year, compounded. After 2 years the population is 50,000 × 1.02 × 1.02 = 52,020.
solution.why_others_wrong: 52,000 adds 2% twice on the original population (no compounding); 48,020 treats the net rate as a 2% fall.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two numbers are 20% and 50% more than a third number respectively. What percentage of the second number is the first number?

solution.concept: Take the third number as 100 to compare the other two
solution.explanation: If the third number is 100, the first is 120 and the second is 150. 120 ÷ 150 × 100 = 80%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 70% subtracts the percentages (100 − 30); 125% is the second number as a percentage of the first.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Sunita's income rises by 20% and her expenditure rises by 12%. As a result her savings rise by 32%. What percentage of her original income did she originally spend?

solution.concept: Income = expenditure + savings, before and after the change
solution.explanation: Take income = 100 and expenditure = E, so savings = 100 − E. After the change, income = 120, expenditure = 1.12E and savings = 1.32(100 − E). So 120 − 1.12E = 132 − 1.32E, giving 0.2E = 12 and E = 60. She spent 60% of her income.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40% is the savings share, not the spending share; 66⅔% and 50% fail the check (savings would change by 36% and 28%).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If A : B = 3 : 4 and B : C = 6 : 7, what is A : B : C?

solution.concept: Make the common term (B) equal in both ratios
solution.explanation: B is 4 in the first ratio and 6 in the second. Make both 12: A : B = 9 : 12 and B : C = 12 : 14. So A : B : C = 9 : 12 : 14.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 : 4 : 7 joins the ratios without matching B; 9 : 12 : 7 scales only the first ratio; 6 : 8 : 7 scales the first ratio by 2 but not the second.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What number must be subtracted from each of 23, 30, 57 and 78 so that the four results are in proportion?

solution.concept: a : b = c : d means a × d = b × c (product of extremes = product of means)
solution.explanation: Let x be subtracted. Then (23 − x)(78 − x) = (30 − x)(57 − x). Expanding, 1794 − 101x + x² = 1710 − 87x + x², so 84 = 14x and x = 6. The numbers become 17, 24, 51, 72, and 17 : 24 = 51 : 72.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4, 5 and 7 fail the check: for example 19 × 74 = 1406 but 26 × 53 = 1378.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: ₹3,800 is divided among A, B and C so that 4 times A's share, 6 times B's share and 9 times C's share are all equal. What is C's share?

solution.explanation: Let 4A = 6B = 9C = k. Then A : B : C = k/4 : k/6 : k/9 = 9 : 6 : 4 (multiplying by 36). C gets 4/19 of ₹3,800 = ₹800.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,800 uses the ratio 4 : 6 : 9 directly instead of the reciprocals; ₹1,200 is B's share.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The present ages of a father and his son are in the ratio 7 : 2, and the product of their ages is 896. What will be the ratio of their ages 6 years from now?

solution.concept: Write the ages as 7k and 2k and use the product to find k
solution.explanation: 7k × 2k = 14k² = 896, so k² = 64 and k = 8. The father is 56 and the son 16. In 6 years they will be 62 and 22, a ratio of 31 : 11.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7 : 2 is the present ratio (a ratio of ages changes with time); 8 : 3 is the ratio after 8 years and 3 : 1 after 4 years.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two numbers are in the ratio 3 : 5. If 9 is subtracted from each, the ratio becomes 12 : 23. What is the smaller number?

solution.concept: Set up one equation in the common multiplier k
solution.explanation: Let the numbers be 3k and 5k. (3k − 9)/(5k − 9) = 12/23 gives 69k − 207 = 60k − 108, so 9k = 99 and k = 11. The smaller number is 33.
solution.why_others_wrong: 55 is the larger number; 27 and 36 fail the check (18 : 36 and 27 : 51 are not 12 : 23).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The sum of the ages of five children born at intervals of 3 years each is 50 years. What is the age of the youngest child?

solution.concept: Ages in arithmetic progression: y, y + 3, y + 6, y + 9, y + 12
solution.explanation: The ages are y, y + 3, y + 6, y + 9 and y + 12, with sum 5y + 30 = 50. So 5y = 20 and y = 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 years is the average (the middle child); 16 years is the eldest.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A is now twice as old as B was when A was as old as B is now. If A is 40 years old now, how old is B now?

solution.concept: Translate each clause; the age gap between two people never changes
solution.explanation: Let B be b years old now. A was b years old 40 − b years ago, and B was then b − (40 − b) = 2b − 40. A's present age is twice that: 40 = 2(2b − 40), so 4b = 120 and b = 30.
steps: A was b years old (40 − b) years ago
Check: 10 years ago A was 30 (B's age now) and B was 20; 40 = 2 × 20
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 years is B's age at that earlier time, not now.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Five years ago, Neha's age was the square of her son's age at that time. Four years from now, Neha will be three times as old as her son. What is Neha's present age?

solution.concept: Let the son's age five years ago be a; Neha's was a². Form a quadratic and keep the positive root
solution.explanation: Now Neha is a² + 5 and her son a + 5. In four years: a² + 9 = 3(a + 9), so a² − 3a − 18 = 0, i.e. (a − 6)(a + 3) = 0 and a = 6. Neha's present age = 36 + 5 = 41.
steps: Five years ago: son a, Neha a²
In 4 years: son a + 9, Neha a² + 9
solution.why_others_wrong: 36 years is her age five years ago; 45 years is her age four years from now; 11 years is the son's present age.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of five numbers is 48. When one number is removed, the average of the remaining four is 45. Which number was removed?

solution.concept: Total = average × count
solution.explanation: Total of five = 5 × 48 = 240. Total of four = 4 × 45 = 180. The removed number is 240 − 180 = 60.
solution.shortcut: The removed number is 48 + 4 × 3 = 60: it is above the old average by 3 for each of the 4 that remain.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 is only the drop in the average; 51 adds 3 to 48 once instead of four times.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A batsman has an average of 42 runs over 16 innings. How many runs must he score in the 17th innings to raise his average to 45?

solution.concept: New total − old total = runs needed in the new innings
solution.explanation: Old total = 16 × 42 = 672. New total needed = 17 × 45 = 765. Runs needed = 765 − 672 = 93.
solution.shortcut: He must score the new average plus 3 for each of the 16 old innings: 45 + 48 = 93.
solution.why_others_wrong: 90 adds 3 × 16 to the old average 42 instead of the new average 45; 45 is the new average itself.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In an office, the 10 officers earn an average of ₹40,000 a month and the other staff earn an average of ₹10,000. The average salary of all employees is ₹15,000. How many other staff are there?

solution.concept: Weighted average: deviations above and below the overall average balance out
solution.explanation: Officers are ₹25,000 above the overall average: 10 × 25,000 = 2,50,000. Each other employee is ₹5,000 below, so their number is 2,50,000 ÷ 5,000 = 50.
solution.shortcut: Alligation: officers : others = (15 − 10) : (40 − 15) = 5 : 25 = 1 : 5, so others = 50.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30, 40 and 60 give overall averages of ₹17,500, ₹16,000 and about ₹14,286.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average age of 8 men rises by 2 years when two of them, aged 21 and 23, are replaced by two women. What is the average age of the two women?

solution.concept: Replacement: increase in total = number of people × increase in average
solution.explanation: The total age rises by 8 × 2 = 16 years. So the women together are 21 + 23 + 16 = 60 years old, an average of 30 years.
solution.why_others_wrong: 23 adds only 2 years to the total; 24 adds 2 to the men's average 22; 38 gives all 16 years to each woman.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of 11 results is 50. The average of the first six is 49 and the average of the last six is 52. What is the sixth result?

solution.concept: The sixth result is counted in both groups of six
solution.explanation: First six total = 294 and last six total = 312. Together they count all 11 results plus the sixth one again, so the sixth = 294 + 312 − 550 = 56.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50.5 averages 49 and 52; 46 subtracts the wrong way (550 − 504).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Sections A, B and C have average marks of 70, 60 and 55. The combined average of A and B is 66, and the combined average of B and C is 57. What is the average mark of all three sections together?

solution.concept: Use each combined average to find the ratio of section sizes, then take the weighted average
solution.explanation: A and B: 70a + 60b = 66(a + b) gives 4a = 6b, so a : b = 3 : 2. B and C: 60b + 55c = 57(b + c) gives 3b = 2c, so b : c = 2 : 3. Hence a : b : c = 3 : 2 : 3 and the overall average is (210 + 120 + 165) ÷ 8 = 61.875.
solution.why_others_wrong: 61.67 is the simple average of 70, 60 and 55, which ignores the different section sizes.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of 25 observations was found to be 36. Later it was noticed that the observation 48 had been recorded as 84 and the observation 25 had been recorded as 52. What is the correct average?

solution.concept: Correct total = wrong total − wrong values + right values
solution.explanation: Wrong total = 25 × 36 = 900. Remove the wrong entries 84 and 52 and add the right ones 48 and 25: 900 − 84 − 52 + 48 + 25 = 837. Correct average = 837 ÷ 25 = 33.48.
solution.why_others_wrong: 34.56 corrects only the first error; 35.64 corrects the first error but adds the second excess instead of removing it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By selling 33 metres of cloth, a shopkeeper gains the selling price of 11 metres. What is his gain percentage?

solution.concept: Gain = SP − CP; express both in terms of the selling price of one metre
solution.explanation: SP of 33 m − CP of 33 m = SP of 11 m, so CP of 33 m = SP of 22 m. The gain is the SP of 11 m on a cost equal to the SP of 22 m: 11/22 = 50%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 33⅓% takes the gain as a percentage of the selling price (11/33) instead of the cost.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: An article costing ₹800 is marked 35% above its cost price and sold for ₹972. What discount percentage was allowed?

solution.concept: Discount % is always calculated on the marked price
solution.explanation: Marked price = 800 × 1.35 = ₹1,080. Discount = 1,080 − 972 = ₹108, which is 108 ÷ 1,080 = 10% of the marked price.
solution.why_others_wrong: 11.11% divides the discount by the selling price; 21.5% is the profit percentage (172 on 800).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shopkeeper uses a weight that reads 1 kg but actually holds 1.1 kg when he buys goods, and a weight that reads 1 kg but holds only 900 g when he sells. He buys and sells at the same price per 'kg'. What is his gain percentage?

solution.concept: Compare the quantity he actually receives with the quantity he actually gives for the same money
solution.explanation: For the price of 1 kg he receives 1,100 g when buying and hands over only 900 g when selling. So the money he gets for 900 g would buy him 1,100 g: gain = 1,100/900 − 1 = 2/9 = 22 2/9%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% adds the two 10% cheats; 21% treats them as successive 10% gains (1.1 × 1.1); 11 1/9% counts only the selling cheat.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sells a bicycle to B at a profit of 25%, and B sells it to C at a profit of 20%. C pays ₹2,250 more than A's cost price. What was A's cost price?

solution.concept: Successive percentage changes multiply
solution.explanation: C pays 1.25 × 1.20 = 1.5 times A's cost, i.e. 50% more. So 50% of A's cost = ₹2,250 and A's cost = ₹4,500.
steps: C's price = A's cost × 1.25 × 1.20 = 1.5 × A's cost
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹5,000 adds the profit percentages (25 + 20 = 45%); ₹6,750 is what C paid.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A dealer sold two mobile phones for ₹2,400 each. On one he gained 20% and on the other he lost 20%. What is his overall gain or loss percentage?

solution.concept: Equal selling prices with equal gain and loss % always give a net loss of (x/10)² %
solution.explanation: Cost of the first = 2,400 ÷ 1.2 = ₹2,000; cost of the second = 2,400 ÷ 0.8 = ₹3,000. Total cost ₹5,000, total sale ₹4,800, so the loss is ₹200, i.e. 4%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'No gain, no loss' assumes the +20% and −20% cancel, but they apply to different cost prices.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shopkeeper marks a lamp 25% above its cost price and allows a discount of 8%. If his profit is ₹156, what is the cost price of the lamp?

solution.concept: Selling price = CP × (1 + markup) × (1 − discount)
solution.explanation: SP = CP × 1.25 × 0.92 = 1.15 × CP, so the profit is 15% of CP. 0.15 × CP = 156 gives CP = ₹1,040.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,248 takes the profit as 12.5%; ₹1,196 is the selling price and ₹1,300 the marked price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A dealer claims to sell rice at a loss of 4% on the cost price, but he gives only 840 g when the customer pays for 1 kg. What is his actual gain or loss percentage?

solution.concept: Actual gain = money received ÷ cost of the quantity actually given
solution.explanation: Let 1 kg cost ₹1,000, so 840 g costs ₹840. He charges 96% of ₹1,000 = ₹960 for those 840 g. Gain = 120 on 840, i.e. 1/7 = 14 2/7%.
steps: Cost of 1 kg = 1,000 ⇒ cost of 840 g = 840
solution.why_others_wrong: 12% subtracts 4 from 16 (the weight cut as a percentage of 1 kg); 19.05% ignores the 4% price cut; 16% is the weight cut alone.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A vendor buys oranges at 5 for ₹12 and sells them at 4 for ₹11. How many oranges must he sell to earn a profit of ₹175?

solution.concept: Profit per article = SP per article − CP per article
solution.explanation: Cost per orange = 12 ÷ 5 = ₹2.40 and selling price per orange = 11 ÷ 4 = ₹2.75, so he gains ₹0.35 per orange. 175 ÷ 0.35 = 500 oranges.
solution.shortcut: Take 20 oranges (LCM of 5 and 4): cost ₹48, sale ₹55, profit ₹7. ₹175 needs 25 × 20 = 500 oranges.
solution.why_others_wrong: 400, 625 and 700 oranges give profits of ₹140, ₹218.75 and ₹245; only 500 oranges give ₹175.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A trader marks his goods a certain percentage above cost. During a festival he allows two successive discounts of 10% and 5% and still makes a profit of 2.6%. By what percentage above cost had he marked the goods?

solution.explanation: Let the cost be 100 and the markup m%. The selling price is 100(1 + m/100) × 0.9 × 0.95 = 0.855 × (100 + m). This equals 102.6, so 100 + m = 120 and m = 20%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 17.6% simply adds 2.6 + 10 + 5; 15% and 25% give profits of −1.675% and +6.875%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A jacket marked at ₹2,400 is sold for ₹2,040. What is the rate of discount?

solution.concept: Discount % = discount ÷ marked price × 100
solution.why_others_wrong: 17.65% divides the discount by the selling price instead of the marked price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What single discount is equivalent to three successive discounts of 20%, 10% and 5%?

solution.concept: Successive discounts multiply the remaining fractions: 0.8 × 0.9 × 0.95
solution.explanation: After the three discounts the customer pays 0.80 × 0.90 × 0.95 = 0.684 of the marked price, so the single equivalent discount is 1 − 0.684 = 31.6%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 35% adds the three rates; 28% stops after the first two discounts.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A store offers 'buy 3, get 1 free' and then a further 10% discount on the bill. Even so, it makes a profit of 17% on its cost. By what percentage above cost are the goods marked?

solution.concept: Convert the offer into an effective selling price per article, then compare with the cost
solution.explanation: For 4 articles the customer pays for 3, less 10%: 3 × 0.9 = 2.7 marked prices. So each article sells for 2.7/4 = 0.675 of its marked price. 0.675 × MP = 1.17 × CP gives MP = 1.7333 × CP, i.e. 73⅓% above cost.
solution.why_others_wrong: 56% ignores the extra 10% discount; 80% adds the two discounts (25% + 10% = 35%) instead of multiplying; 30% ignores the free article.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: At what rate of simple interest per annum will ₹6,400 amount to ₹8,320 in 4 years?

solution.concept: SI = P × R × T ÷ 100, with SI = amount − principal
solution.why_others_wrong: 30% is the total interest over 4 years as a percentage of the principal, not the yearly rate.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sum of money lent at simple interest amounts to ₹9,800 in 5 years and to ₹12,005 in 8 years. What is the rate of interest per annum?

solution.concept: The difference of two amounts is the interest for the difference in years
solution.explanation: Interest for 3 years = 12,005 − 9,800 = ₹2,205, so one year's interest is ₹735. The principal is 9,800 − 5 × 735 = ₹6,125, and the rate is 735 ÷ 6,125 × 100 = 12%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7.5% divides the yearly interest by the 5-year amount (₹9,800) instead of the principal.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A bank charges simple interest at r% per annum for the first 3 years, (r + 2)% for the next 4 years and (r + 4)% for the 3 years after that. If the total interest for the 10 years is 92% of the principal, what is r?

solution.concept: Total SI % = Σ (rate × years) for each period
solution.explanation: Total interest as a percentage of the principal = 3r + 4(r + 2) + 3(r + 4) = 10r + 20. Setting 10r + 20 = 92 gives r = 7.2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9.2 forgets the extra 2% and 4% (10r = 92); 7.5 gives 95%, and 6.5 gives 85%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What equal annual instalment, paid at the end of each year, will discharge a debt of ₹6,450 due in 4 years at 5% per annum simple interest?

solution.concept: Each instalment earns simple interest from its payment date to the due date; their total equals the debt
solution.explanation: Let each instalment be x. The first earns interest for 3 years, the second for 2, the third for 1 and the fourth for none. Total value at the due date = 4x + x × 5% × (3 + 2 + 1) = 4x + 0.3x = 4.3x = 6,450, so x = ₹1,500.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,612.50 divides the debt by 4 and ignores interest on the instalments; ₹1,290 divides by 5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: At what rate of compound interest per annum, compounded annually, will ₹6,400 become ₹7,744 in 2 years?

solution.concept: A = P(1 + R/100)ⁿ; take the square root of A/P
solution.why_others_wrong: 10.5% is the simple-interest rate for the same amounts; 21% is the total growth over two years.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the compound interest on ₹16,000 for 9 months at 20% per annum, compounded quarterly.

solution.concept: Quarterly compounding: rate ÷ 4 per quarter, number of quarters as the exponent
solution.explanation: The quarterly rate is 20 ÷ 4 = 5% and 9 months = 3 quarters. Amount = 16,000 × 1.05³ = 16,000 × 1.157625 = ₹18,522, so CI = ₹2,522.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,400 is simple interest; ₹1,640 counts only 2 quarters.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The simple interest on a sum for 2 years is ₹1,600 and the compound interest on it for 2 years at the same rate (compounded annually) is ₹1,680. What is the sum?

solution.concept: CI − SI for 2 years = interest earned in year 2 on the first year's interest
solution.explanation: SI for one year = 1,600 ÷ 2 = ₹800. The extra ₹80 in CI is interest on that ₹800 for one year, so the rate is 80 ÷ 800 = 10%. Then the sum = 800 ÷ 10% = ₹8,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹16,000 uses the 2-year SI (₹1,600) as one year's interest; ₹4,000 uses a 20% rate.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: On ₹25,000 at 20% per annum for 2 years, by how much does the compound interest compounded half-yearly exceed the compound interest compounded annually?

solution.concept: Half-yearly: rate/2 per half-year, 2n half-years
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹250 is the difference for 1 year only; ₹1,602.50 compares the half-yearly CI with simple interest.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: P, Q and R invest ₹18,000, ₹27,000 and ₹36,000 in a business for a year. At the end of the year R gets ₹4,800 more than P. What is the total profit?

solution.concept: Profit is shared in the ratio of capitals when the time is the same
solution.explanation: Capitals are in the ratio 18 : 27 : 36 = 2 : 3 : 4. R gets 2 parts more than P, so 2 parts = ₹4,800 and one part = ₹2,400. Total = 9 parts = ₹21,600.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹43,200 treats ₹4,800 as one part instead of two; ₹14,400 is P's and R's combined share (6 parts), not the total.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Asha starts a business with ₹40,000. Bharat joins after 3 months with ₹60,000 and Chetan joins after 6 months with ₹80,000. Out of a profit of ₹50,000 at the end of the year, what is Bharat's share?

solution.concept: Profit share ∝ capital × months invested
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹16,000 is Asha's (or Chetan's) share; ₹16,667 ignores time and uses the capital ratio 2 : 3 : 4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The capitals of A and B are in the ratio 5 : 6 and their profits are in the ratio 2 : 3. If A's capital was invested for 8 months, for how many months was B's capital invested?

solution.concept: Profit ratio = (capital × time) ratio
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 months assumes B stayed the full year; 8 months assumes equal time, which would give a 5 : 6 profit ratio.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Anil and Bimal invest ₹60,000 and ₹90,000 in a shop. Anil runs the shop and draws ₹1,500 a month as salary; the remaining profit is shared in the ratio of capitals. If the profit for the year is ₹1,08,000, how much does Anil receive in all?

solution.concept: Pay the working partner's salary first, then divide the rest by capital
solution.explanation: Salary for the year = 1,500 × 12 = ₹18,000. Remaining profit = ₹90,000, shared 2 : 3, so Anil gets ₹36,000 more. Total = 18,000 + 36,000 = ₹54,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹43,200 ignores the salary; ₹36,000 leaves out the salary from the total; ₹61,200 adds the salary but shares the whole profit before deducting it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Ajay starts a business with ₹45,000. Some months later Bina joins with ₹60,000, and 2 months after Bina, Charu joins with ₹90,000. At the end of the year the profits of Ajay and Bina are in the ratio 3 : 2. Out of a total profit of ₹1,26,000, what is Charu's share?

solution.concept: Find the unknown joining month from the given profit ratio, then share by capital × months
solution.explanation: Ajay: 45 × 12 = 540. If Bina stays t months, 540 : 60t = 3 : 2, so 60t = 360 and t = 6 (she joins after 6 months). Charu joins 2 months later and stays 4 months: 90 × 4 = 360. Ratio 540 : 360 : 360 = 3 : 2 : 2, so Charu gets 2/7 of ₹1,26,000 = ₹36,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹54,000 is Ajay's share; ₹42,000 gives Charu 6 months, like Bina, instead of 4 (ratio 540 : 360 : 540).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In a firm, A's capital is 1.5 times B's capital, and C's capital is 40% of A's and B's capitals together. All three invest for the same period. Out of a profit of ₹84,000, what is C's share?

solution.concept: Express every capital in terms of one of them
solution.explanation: Let B = 2x, so A = 3x. A + B = 5x and C = 40% of 5x = 2x. Ratio A : B : C = 3 : 2 : 2, so C gets 2/7 of ₹84,000 = ₹24,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹33,600 is 40% of the profit; ₹36,000 is A's share.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In what ratio must water be mixed with milk costing ₹60 per litre so that the mixture is worth ₹48 per litre?

solution.concept: Alligation: water costs ₹0 per litre
solution.explanation: By alligation, water : milk = (60 − 48) : (48 − 0) = 12 : 48 = 1 : 4.
steps: Check: 4 litres of milk cost ₹240; 5 litres of mixture at ₹48 = ₹240
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 : 1 is the ratio reversed (milk : water).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many litres of a 70% alcohol solution must be added to 30 litres of a 40% alcohol solution to get a 50% alcohol solution?

solution.concept: Alligation on concentrations, or a balance of pure alcohol
solution.explanation: By alligation, 40% : 70% solution = (70 − 50) : (50 − 40) = 2 : 1. With 30 litres of the 40% solution, the 70% solution needed is 15 litres.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 litres gives 47.5%; 20 litres gives 52%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A cask holds 50 litres of pure juice. Some juice is drawn off and replaced with water; then the same quantity of the mixture is drawn off and replaced with water again. Juice and water are now in the ratio 16 : 9. How many litres were drawn off each time?

solution.concept: After n replacements, juice left = initial × (1 − x/V)ⁿ
solution.explanation: Juice left is 16/25 of the cask, so (1 − x/50)² = 16/25. Then 1 − x/50 = 4/5, x/50 = 1/5 and x = 10 litres.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 litres gives juice : water = 9 : 16 (the ratio reversed); 8 and 12.5 litres give 441 : 184 and 9 : 7.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A is three times as efficient as B. Working together they finish a job in 12 days. In how many days can A alone finish it?

solution.concept: Work = efficiency × time
solution.explanation: Let B do 1 unit a day, so A does 3. Together they do 4 units a day for 12 days, i.e. 48 units. A alone takes 48 ÷ 3 = 16 days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 48 days is B's time alone; 36 days multiplies 12 by 3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: 16 workers can build a wall in 15 days working 9 hours a day. In how many days can 20 workers build the same wall working 8 hours a day?

solution.concept: M₁ × D₁ × H₁ = M₂ × D₂ × H₂ for the same work
solution.explanation: Total work = 16 × 15 × 9 = 2,160 worker-hours. 20 workers working 8 hours a day put in 160 worker-hours a day, so they need 2,160 ÷ 160 = 13.5 days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 days ignores the change in hours; 10⅔ days swaps the hours (multiplies by 8/9 instead of 9/8).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: One man does as much work as two boys. 6 men and 8 boys can finish a job in 10 days. How long will 4 men and 4 boys take to finish it?

solution.concept: Convert everyone into one unit (boy-units)
solution.explanation: 6 men + 8 boys = 12 + 8 = 20 boy-units, so the job is 20 × 10 = 200 boy-days. 4 men + 4 boys = 12 boy-units, so they need 200 ÷ 12 = 16⅔ days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 days counts 4 men + 4 boys as 10 boy-units; 12½ days counts them as 16.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A completes 40% of a job in 8 days and then leaves. B completes the remaining job in 18 days. In how many days would A and B together have finished the whole job?

solution.concept: Find each person's full-job time from the part done
solution.explanation: A does 40% in 8 days, so A alone needs 20 days. B does 60% in 18 days, so B alone needs 30 days. Together: 1/20 + 1/30 = 1/12, i.e. 12 days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 days averages 20 and 30; 13 days averages the given 8 and 18 days.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: 3 men and 4 women together earn ₹3,780 in 7 days, while 11 men and 13 women together earn ₹15,040 in 8 days. In how many days will 5 men and 10 women together earn ₹8,800?

solution.concept: Form two equations in the daily wages of a man (m) and a woman (w)
solution.explanation: Daily: 3m + 4w = 540 and 11m + 13w = 1,880. Multiplying the first by 13 and the second by 4 and subtracting gives 5m = 500, so m = ₹100 and w = ₹60. 5 men and 10 women earn 500 + 600 = ₹1,100 a day, so ₹8,800 takes 8 days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6, 10 and 11 days would need daily earnings of about ₹1,467, ₹880 and ₹800; the wages found give ₹1,100 a day.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A is 50% more efficient than B, and C is half as efficient as B. Working together, A, B and C finish a project in 16 days. How many days would A and C together take?

solution.concept: Efficiency ratios give a common unit of work
solution.explanation: Let B do 2 units a day. Then A does 3 and C does 1. Together they do 6 units a day, so the project is 6 × 16 = 96 units. A and C do 4 units a day, so they need 96 ÷ 4 = 24 days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 32 days is A's time alone; 20 days drops C's contribution from the total but not from the pair.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Pipe A can fill a tank in 15 minutes and pipe B in 20 minutes. If both are opened together on the empty tank, how long will they take to fill it?

solution.concept: Add the filling rates (fractions of the tank per minute)
solution.explanation: Together they fill 1/15 + 1/20 = (4 + 3)/60 = 7/60 of the tank per minute, so they take 60/7 = 8 4/7 minutes.
steps: A: 1/15 per minute; B: 1/20 per minute
solution.why_others_wrong: 17½ minutes averages the two times; 35 minutes adds them.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two pipes can fill a tank in 12 hours and 15 hours. Because of a leak, the two pipes together take 8 hours to fill it. In how many hours can the leak alone empty the full tank?

solution.concept: Leak rate = (rate without leak) − (rate with leak)
solution.explanation: Without the leak the pipes fill 1/12 + 1/15 = 9/60 = 3/20 of the tank per hour. With the leak they fill 1/8. So the leak empties 3/20 − 1/8 = 1/40 per hour, i.e. the full tank in 40 hours.
steps: Leak empties the tank in 40 hours
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 hours compares the 8-hour rate with the first pipe alone (1/8 − 1/12 = 1/24); the leak works against both pipes together, so its rate is 3/20 − 1/8.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 24 minutes and 32 minutes. Both are opened together on the empty tank. After how many minutes should B be closed so that the tank is full exactly 18 minutes after the start?

solution.concept: Each pipe's contribution = its rate × the time it stays open
solution.explanation: A runs for all 18 minutes and fills 18/24 = 3/4 of the tank. B must fill the remaining 1/4, which takes 32 × 1/4 = 8 minutes. So B is closed after 8 minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 and 10 minutes leave the tank at 15/16 full or overflowing by 1/16 at 18 minutes.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A car covers 150 km at 50 km/h and then 200 km at 40 km/h. What is its average speed for the whole journey?

solution.concept: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time (not the average of the speeds)
solution.explanation: Time for the first part = 150 ÷ 50 = 3 hours; for the second part = 200 ÷ 40 = 5 hours. Average speed = 350 ÷ 8 = 43.75 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 45 km/h averages the two speeds; 44.44 km/h uses the equal-distance formula 2ab/(a + b), but the distances are not equal.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two friends start walking from the same point in the same direction at 5 km/h and 7.5 km/h. How far apart will they be after 3 hours 12 minutes?

solution.concept: Same direction: relative speed = difference of speeds
solution.explanation: The gap grows at 7.5 − 5 = 2.5 km/h. 3 hours 12 minutes = 3.2 hours, so the gap is 2.5 × 3.2 = 8 km.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40 km adds the speeds (that is for opposite directions); 7.5 km uses only 3 hours.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A bus goes from town P to town Q at 48 km/h and returns along the same route. Its average speed for the round trip is 57.6 km/h. What was its speed on the return journey?

solution.concept: For equal distances, average speed = 2ab ÷ (a + b)
solution.why_others_wrong: 67.2 km/h assumes the average is the mean of the two speeds (2 × 57.6 − 48).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two people start at the same time from towns 72 km apart and walk towards each other at 5 km/h and 7 km/h. A dog starts with the first person, runs to the second at 15 km/h, turns back at once, and keeps running between them until they meet. What total distance does the dog run?

solution.concept: The dog runs for exactly as long as the two people take to meet
solution.explanation: The people close the gap at 5 + 7 = 12 km/h, so they meet after 72 ÷ 12 = 6 hours. The dog runs at 15 km/h for those 6 hours: 15 × 6 = 90 km.
steps: Relative speed of the people = 12 km/h
solution.shortcut: Do not trace each leg of the dog's run; only the total time matters.
solution.why_others_wrong: 72 km is the distance between the towns; 60 km uses the dog's speed relative to one walker (15 − 5) × 6.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two runners start together from the same point on a 600 m circular track and run in the same direction at 5 m/s and 7 m/s. After how long will they first be together again at the starting point?

solution.concept: Meeting at the start: LCM of the lap times; meeting anywhere: track length ÷ relative speed
solution.explanation: Lap times are 600 ÷ 5 = 120 s and 600 ÷ 7 = 600/7 s. They are both at the start when each has completed a whole number of laps: after 600 s the first has done 5 laps and the second 7 laps, and no earlier time works. 600 s = 10 minutes.
steps: Check: in 600 s, 5 laps and 7 laps
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 minutes is when they first meet anywhere on the track (600 ÷ (7 − 5) = 300 s), which is not the start point; 2 minutes is only the first runner's lap time.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two cars start at the same time from points A and B, 300 km apart. If they drive towards each other they meet in 2.5 hours; if they drive in the same direction, the faster one catches the slower one in 15 hours. What is the speed of the faster car?

solution.concept: Towards each other: sum of speeds; same direction: difference of speeds
solution.explanation: Sum of speeds = 300 ÷ 2.5 = 120 km/h and difference = 300 ÷ 15 = 20 km/h. The faster car's speed is (120 + 20) ÷ 2 = 70 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 km/h is the slower car; 60 km/h is half the sum of the speeds.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat's speed in still water is 18 km/h and the stream flows at 4 km/h. How far will the boat travel downstream in 2 hours 30 minutes?

solution.concept: Downstream speed = boat speed + stream speed
solution.explanation: Downstream speed = 18 + 4 = 22 km/h. In 2.5 hours the boat covers 22 × 2.5 = 55 km.
solution.why_others_wrong: 35 km uses the upstream speed (14 km/h); 45 km ignores the stream.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A man rows to a place 48 km away and back in 14 hours. He finds that he can row 4 km downstream in the same time as 3 km upstream. What is the speed of the stream?

solution.concept: Equal times for 4 km and 3 km mean downstream : upstream speed = 4 : 3
solution.explanation: Let the speeds be 4k and 3k. Then 48/(4k) + 48/(3k) = 12/k + 16/k = 28/k = 14, so k = 2. Downstream = 8 km/h, upstream = 6 km/h, and the stream's speed = (8 − 6) ÷ 2 = 1 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 km/h forgets to halve the difference; 7 km/h is the man's rowing speed in still water.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat takes twice as long to go a certain distance upstream as to go the same distance downstream. If its speed in still water is 9 km/h, what is the speed of the stream?

solution.concept: Same distance: time is inversely proportional to speed
solution.explanation: Twice the time upstream means the downstream speed is twice the upstream speed: 9 + s = 2(9 − s), so 3s = 9 and s = 3 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.5 km/h halves the boat's speed; 6 km/h is the upstream speed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat goes 30 km upstream and 44 km downstream in 10 hours. It also goes 40 km upstream and 55 km downstream in 13 hours. What is the speed of the boat in still water?

solution.concept: Treat 1/upstream speed and 1/downstream speed as the unknowns
solution.explanation: Let a = 1/u and b = 1/d. Then 30a + 44b = 10 and 40a + 55b = 13. Multiplying the first by 4 and the second by 3: 120a + 176b = 40 and 120a + 165b = 39, so 11b = 1, b = 1/11 and d = 11 km/h. Then 30a = 10 − 4 = 6, a = 1/5 and u = 5 km/h. Boat speed = (11 + 5) ÷ 2 = 8 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 11 km/h and 5 km/h are the downstream and upstream speeds; 3 km/h is the stream.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A train running at 72 km/h crosses a platform in 30 seconds and a man standing on the platform in 18 seconds. What is the length of the platform?

solution.concept: Crossing a man covers the train's length; crossing a platform covers train + platform
solution.explanation: 72 km/h = 20 m/s. The train's length = 20 × 18 = 360 m, and train + platform = 20 × 30 = 600 m. So the platform is 600 − 360 = 240 m.
solution.shortcut: The extra 12 seconds are spent on the platform alone: 20 × 12 = 240 m.
solution.why_others_wrong: 360 m is the train's length; 600 m is train + platform.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two trains of equal length run on parallel tracks in the same direction at 46 km/h and 36 km/h. The faster train passes the slower one completely in 36 seconds. What is the length of each train?

solution.concept: Overtaking: relative speed = difference; distance = sum of the two lengths
solution.explanation: Relative speed = 10 km/h = 25/9 m/s. In 36 seconds the faster train gains 25/9 × 36 = 100 m, which equals the two lengths together. Each train is 50 m long.
solution.why_others_wrong: 100 m is the combined length; 82 m uses the sum of speeds (82 km/h) as a distance.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A train passes a man walking at 3 km/h in the same direction in 10 seconds, and passes another man walking at 5 km/h in the opposite direction in 9 seconds. What is the length of the train?

solution.concept: Same direction: subtract the man's speed; opposite direction: add it. The train's length is the same both times
solution.explanation: Let the train's speed be v km/h. (v − 3) × 10 = (v + 5) × 9 (both in km/h × seconds), so v = 75 km/h. The length is (75 − 3) × 5/18 × 10 = 20 × 10 = 200 m.
steps: Relative speed with first man = 72 km/h = 20 m/s
solution.why_others_wrong: 180 m, 225 m and 250 m fail the check: with 10 s for the first man they give train speeds of 67.8, 84 and 93 km/h, which do not give 9 s for the second man.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The diagonals of a rhombus are 24 cm and 18 cm. What is its perimeter?

solution.concept: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles
solution.explanation: Half-diagonals are 12 cm and 9 cm, so each side = √(12² + 9²) = √225 = 15 cm. Perimeter = 4 × 15 = 60 cm.
solution.why_others_wrong: 84 cm doubles the sum of the diagonals; 216 is the area in cm²; 42 cm adds the diagonals.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The total surface area of a cube is 486 cm². What is its volume?

solution.concept: Total surface area of a cube = 6a²; volume = a³
solution.explanation: 6a² = 486 gives a² = 81 and a = 9 cm. Volume = 9³ = 729 cm³.
solution.why_others_wrong: 81 is the area of one face; 1,331 and 512 are the cubes of 11 and 8.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A cone has a base radius of 7 cm and a height of 24 cm. What is its curved surface area? (Use π = 22/7.)

solution.concept: Curved surface area of a cone = πrl, where l = √(r² + h²) is the slant height
solution.why_others_wrong: 528 cm² uses the height instead of the slant height; 704 cm² is the total surface area (adds the base); 1,232 cm³ is the volume.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The length of a rectangle is increased by 20% and its breadth is decreased by 20%. What is the effect on its area?

solution.concept: New area = (1 + a)(1 − b) × old area
solution.explanation: New area = 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96 times the old area, i.e. a 4% decrease.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'No change' assumes +20% and −20% cancel; they do not, because the 20% decrease applies to a larger base.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Rain falls on a flat rectangular roof 44 m long and 21 m wide to a depth of 5 cm. All the water flows into an empty cylindrical tank with a base radius of 3.5 m. How high will the water rise in the tank? (Use π = 22/7.)

solution.concept: Volume of rain on the roof = volume of water in the tank
solution.explanation: Rain volume = 44 × 21 × 0.05 = 46.2 m³. Tank base area = 22/7 × 3.5² = 38.5 m². Height = 46.2 ÷ 38.5 = 1.2 m.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 m converts 5 cm to 0.5 m; 0.3 m uses 7 m (the diameter) as the radius; 2.4 m doubles the answer.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A right circular cone is cut by a plane parallel to its base through the midpoint of its height. What is the ratio of the volume of the small cone cut off to the volume of the remaining frustum?

solution.concept: Similar solids: volumes scale as the cube of the linear ratio
solution.explanation: The small cone is similar to the original with half its height and half its radius, so its volume is (1/2)³ = 1/8 of the original. The frustum is the remaining 7/8, giving 1 : 7.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 8 compares the small cone with the whole cone, not with the frustum; 1 : 3 uses the area ratio 1 : 4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Three fair coins are tossed together. What is the probability of getting at least two heads?

solution.concept: List the 8 equally likely outcomes and count the favourable ones
solution.explanation: Of the 8 outcomes, three have exactly two heads (HHT, HTH, THH) and one has three heads (HHH). So 4 of the 8 are favourable: 4/8 = 1/2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3/8 counts exactly two heads only; 7/8 is the probability of at least one head.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: One card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 cards. What is the probability that it is a face card or a spade?

solution.concept: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)
solution.explanation: There are 12 face cards and 13 spades, but 3 cards (the jack, queen and king of spades) are in both groups. Favourable cards = 12 + 13 − 3 = 22, so P = 22/52 = 11/26.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25/52 counts the three spade face cards twice; 3/13 counts face cards only; 1/4 counts spades only.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A bag contains 4 red, 5 green and 6 yellow balls. Two balls are drawn at random together. What is the probability that both are of the same colour?

solution.concept: Count selections: ⁿC₂ for each colour over ¹⁵C₂ in all
solution.explanation: Total ways = ¹⁵C₂ = 105. Same colour: ⁴C₂ + ⁵C₂ + ⁶C₂ = 6 + 10 + 15 = 31. P = 31/105.
steps: Both red: ⁴C₂ = 6; both green: ⁵C₂ = 10; both yellow: ⁶C₂ = 15
solution.why_others_wrong: 77/225 draws with replacement; 74/105 is the probability that the colours differ.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the two numbers differ by at most 1?

solution.concept: 'At most 1' means a difference of 0 or 1
solution.explanation: Difference 0: 6 outcomes (1-1, …, 6-6). Difference 1: 5 pairs in each order, 10 outcomes. Favourable = 16 of 36, so P = 4/9.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5/18 counts only a difference of exactly 1; 1/6 counts only equal numbers; 11/36 counts each difference-1 pair in one order only.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A fair coin is tossed four times. What is the probability that no two consecutive tosses are both heads?

solution.concept: Count sequences directly (or build them toss by toss)
solution.explanation: Count the sequences with no 'HH': 0 heads: 1 (TTTT); 1 head: 4; 2 non-adjacent heads: HTHT, HTTH, THTH = 3. 3 or 4 heads always have two adjacent heads. Total = 8 of 16, so P = 1/2.
steps: Two heads, not adjacent: HTHT, HTTH, THTH = 3
solution.why_others_wrong: 5/16 counts only sequences with at most one head; 3/8 counts only those with exactly two heads (6/16).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Three cards are drawn together at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 cards. What is the probability that they are all from different suits?

solution.concept: Choose the 3 suits, then one card from each; divide by ⁵²C₃
solution.why_others_wrong: 3/8 assumes the cards are drawn with replacement (1 × 3/4 × 2/4); 2197/22100 forgets to choose which 3 of the 4 suits appear.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Bag A has 3 white and 2 black balls; bag B has 2 white and 4 black balls. One bag is chosen at random and a ball drawn from it is white. What is the probability that it came from bag A?

solution.concept: Conditional probability (Bayes): P(A | white) = P(A and white) ÷ P(white)
solution.why_others_wrong: 3/5 is P(white | A), the reverse condition; 7/15 is the overall probability of drawing white; 1/2 ignores the evidence that the ball is white.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Three fair dice are rolled together. What is the probability that the total is 10?

solution.concept: Count ordered triples (a, b, c) with a + b + c = 10, each from 1 to 6
solution.explanation: Group by the first die a: the other two must add to 10 − a. a = 1: 4 ways; a = 2: 5; a = 3: 6; a = 4: 5; a = 5: 4; a = 6: 3. Total = 27 of the 216 outcomes, so P = 27/216 = 1/8.
steps: a = 2 needs b + c = 8: 5 ways; a = 3 needs 7: 6 ways; a = 4 needs 6: 5 ways
a = 5 needs 5: 4 ways; a = 6 needs 4: 3 ways
solution.why_others_wrong: 25/216 is the probability of a total of 9, which looks similar but has fewer combinations.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many 4-digit numbers can be formed using the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 if no digit is repeated?

solution.concept: Permutations: ⁿPᵣ = n × (n − 1) × … (r factors)
solution.explanation: The thousands digit has 6 choices, the hundreds 5, the tens 4 and the units 3: 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 = 360.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,296 allows repetition (6⁴); 15 counts selections (⁶C₄), not arrangements; 720 is 6!.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many ways can the letters of the word DEPOSIT be arranged so that the vowels occupy only the odd positions (1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th)?

solution.concept: Place the restricted letters first, then arrange the rest
solution.explanation: DEPOSIT has 7 different letters, with vowels E, O, I. The 3 vowels go into 3 of the 4 odd places in ⁴P₃ = 24 ways. The 4 consonants fill the remaining 4 places in 4! = 24 ways. Total = 24 × 24 = 576.
steps: Vowels E, O, I into odd places: ⁴P₃ = 24
Consonants D, P, S, T into the other 4 places: 4! = 24
solution.why_others_wrong: 720 is the count with the vowels together; 144 = 3! × 4! forgets that the vowels can choose 3 of 4 odd places; 5,040 has no restriction.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A committee of 5 is to be chosen from 7 men and 4 women so that it includes at least 3 women. In how many ways can this be done?

solution.concept: 'At least' means adding the separate cases
solution.explanation: Case 3 women + 2 men: ⁴C₃ × ⁷C₂ = 4 × 21 = 84. Case 4 women + 1 man: ⁴C₄ × ⁷C₁ = 7. Total = 91.
solution.why_others_wrong: 84 counts only exactly 3 women; 462 = ¹¹C₅ has no restriction; 140 = ⁴C₃ × ⁷C₃ is a 6-member committee.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many ways can 5 boys and 5 girls sit around a circular table so that no two girls sit next to each other? (Arrangements that differ only by a rotation are the same.)

solution.concept: Seat one group around the circle first ((n − 1)! ways), then place the other group in the gaps
solution.explanation: Seat the 5 boys around the table in (5 − 1)! = 24 ways. This leaves 5 gaps between boys, and the 5 girls fill them in 5! = 120 ways. Total = 24 × 120 = 2,880.
solution.why_others_wrong: 14,400 = 5! × 5! treats the table as a row of fixed seats with the boys first; 28,800 doubles that; 576 = 4! × 4! fixes a girl as well.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the total production of mustard in the five villages together?

solution.concept: Column total
solution.explanation: Add the Mustard column: 85 + 60 + 95 + 70 + 90 = 400 tonnes.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which village had the highest total production of the four crops?

solution.concept: Row totals
solution.explanation: Row totals: Amarpur 950, Bhatpur 1,000, Chandpur 1,040, Dharampur 800 and Eklapur 1,080 tonnes. Eklapur is highest.
solution.why_others_wrong: Chandpur has the highest wheat and pulses output, but not the highest total.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Rice production in Eklapur is what percentage more than rice production in Amarpur?

solution.concept: Percentage more = difference ÷ base × 100 (base = the village after 'than')
solution.explanation: Eklapur 400 and Amarpur 320 tonnes. The difference, 80, is 80 ÷ 320 = 25% of Amarpur's output.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% uses Eklapur (400) as the base; 125% is Eklapur's output as a percentage of Amarpur's.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the ratio of the wheat production of Chandpur and Dharampur together to the pulses production of all five villages together?

solution.concept: Ratio of a partial column sum to a full column sum
solution.explanation: Wheat of Chandpur and Dharampur = 510 + 290 = 800. Pulses of all five = 125 + 110 + 155 + 80 + 140 = 610. 800 : 610 = 80 : 61.
solution.why_others_wrong: 61 : 80 is reversed; 40 : 31 uses a pulses total of 620.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average pulses production per village is what percentage of the average mustard production per village?

solution.concept: Averages over the same number of villages compare like totals
solution.explanation: Both averages divide by 5, so the comparison is 610 ÷ 400 × 100 = 152.5%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 65.57% is mustard as a percentage of pulses; 52.5% is how much more pulses there are; 122 is the pulses average itself.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the room revenue of Pine View in June 2026?

solution.concept: Revenue = rooms × occupancy × days × tariff
solution.explanation: Pine View sells 80 × 90% = 72 rooms a night, i.e. 72 × 30 = 2,160 room-nights in June. At ₹4,500 each, revenue = ₹97,20,000 = ₹97.2 lakh.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹108 lakh assumes 100% occupancy; ₹100.44 lakh uses 31 days; ₹3.24 lakh is one night's revenue.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Heritage's room revenue in June was what percentage more than Sagar's?

solution.concept: Compute both revenues, then 'percent more than' on Sagar's base
solution.explanation: Heritage: 60 × 85% × 30 = 1,530 room-nights × ₹6,000 = ₹91.8 lakh. Sagar: 120 × 75% × 30 = 2,700 × ₹3,200 = ₹86.4 lakh. Difference ₹5.4 lakh, which is 5.4 ÷ 86.4 = 6.25% of Sagar's revenue.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.88% uses Heritage as the base; 87.5% compares the tariffs only (6,000 vs 3,200).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: On an average night in June, what percentage of all the rooms of the five hotels together were occupied?

solution.concept: A combined percentage is a weighted average, weighted by the number of rooms
solution.explanation: Occupied rooms per night: Sagar 90, Pine View 72, Lotus 90, Heritage 51 and Orchid 63, total 366 of 500 rooms. 366 ÷ 500 = 73.2%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 76% is the simple average of the five occupancy percentages, which ignores the different hotel sizes.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If Lotus had achieved an average occupancy of 72% in June at the same tariff, by how much would its room revenue have increased?

solution.concept: Extra revenue = rooms × extra occupancy × days × tariff
solution.explanation: Occupancy rises by 12 percentage points: 150 × 12% = 18 more rooms a night, i.e. 540 more room-nights in June. At ₹2,800 each, that is ₹15,12,000 = ₹15.12 lakh.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹9.072 lakh raises revenue by 12% instead of by 12 percentage points of occupancy; ₹90.72 lakh is the new total revenue, not the increase.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In September 2026 (30 days), Pine View cut its tariff by 10% and its occupancy rose to 95%. By what percentage did its room revenue change compared with June?

solution.concept: Revenue ∝ occupancy × tariff when rooms and days are unchanged
solution.explanation: Revenue changes by the factor (95/90) × 0.90 = 0.95, a 5% decrease. Directly: 80 × 95% × 30 = 2,280 room-nights × ₹4,050 = ₹92.34 lakh, against ₹97.2 lakh in June.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.56% increase counts only the higher occupancy; 10% decrease counts only the tariff cut.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the total number of visitors in 2022 and 2023 together?

solution.concept: Read two bars and add; values are in thousands
solution.explanation: 2022: 90 thousand and 2023: 108 thousand. Together 198 thousand = 1,98,000 visitors.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18,000 is the difference between the two years, not the total.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage did the number of visitors fall from 2020 to 2021?

solution.concept: Percentage decrease = fall ÷ earlier value × 100
solution.explanation: Visitors fell from 72 thousand to 54 thousand, a fall of 18 thousand, which is 18 ÷ 72 = 25% of the 2020 figure.
solution.why_others_wrong: 33⅓% uses 2021 as the base; 18% is the fall in thousands, not a percentage; 75% is 2021 as a percentage of 2020.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the average number of visitors per year over the six years?

solution.concept: Average = total ÷ number of years
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,15,800 divides by 5 instead of 6; 1,01,400 averages only 2021 to 2025.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the ratio of the total visitors in 2021 and 2022 together to the total visitors in 2024 and 2025 together?

solution.concept: Ratio of two sums, reduced to lowest terms
solution.why_others_wrong: 85 : 48 is reversed; 8 : 15 uses 270 (2 × 135) for the second sum.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The ticket price was ₹80 in 2024 and was raised by 35% for 2025. By what percentage did the museum's ticket revenue change from 2024 to 2025? (Assume every visitor bought one ticket.)

solution.concept: Revenue = visitors × price; combine the two changes multiplicatively
solution.why_others_wrong: 35% ignores the fall in visitors; 23.89% adds the percentage changes (+35% and −11.11%) instead of multiplying the factors.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many non-fiction books did the four bookstores sell in all?

solution.concept: Add one segment across all bars
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,860 is the fiction total; 3,400 is all books.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What percentage of the books sold by Readwell were fiction?

solution.concept: Segment ÷ bar total × 100
solution.explanation: Readwell sold 600 fiction out of 1,000 books, i.e. 60%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40% is the non-fiction share; 150% is fiction as a percentage of non-fiction.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the ratio of the fiction books sold by Kitab Ghar and Bookmark together to the non-fiction books sold by Page Turner and Readwell together?

solution.concept: Pick the right segment from each bar
solution.explanation: Fiction of Kitab Ghar + Bookmark = 480 + 420 = 900. Non-fiction of Page Turner + Readwell = 540 + 400 = 940. 900 : 940 = 45 : 47.
solution.why_others_wrong: 47 : 45 is reversed; 9 : 10 uses 1,000 (Readwell's total) in place of the non-fiction sum.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Fiction books sell at an average of ₹250 and non-fiction books at an average of ₹400. What was the total revenue of the four bookstores from these sales?

solution.concept: Revenue by category = units × average price; the categories have different volumes, so do not average the prices
