solution.why_others_wrong: ₹11.05 lakh multiplies all 3,400 books by the simple average price ₹325; ₹11.29 lakh swaps the two prices; ₹6.16 lakh is the non-fiction revenue alone.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many employees work in the IT department?

solution.concept: Slice value = total × percentage
solution.why_others_wrong: 792 takes the total as 3,600; 700 uses 20%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the ratio of the number of employees in Marketing to the number in HR and Finance together?

solution.concept: With a common total, ratios of counts equal ratios of percentages
solution.explanation: Marketing 14% against HR + Finance = 6% + 12% = 18%. 14 : 18 = 7 : 9 (490 : 630 employees).
solution.why_others_wrong: 9 : 7 is reversed; 7 : 6 compares Marketing with Finance only; 7 : 3 with HR only.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: 25% of the Production employees and 40% of the IT employees are women. What percentage of the employees of these two departments together are women?

solution.concept: Weighted average of the two percentages, weighted by department size
solution.explanation: Women: 25% of 980 = 245 in Production and 40% of 770 = 308 in IT, total 553. The two departments have 980 + 770 = 1,750 employees, so 553 ÷ 1,750 = 31.6%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 32.5% is the simple average of 25% and 40%; 15.8% divides by all 3,500 employees; 65% adds the two percentages.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many units did brand Q sell in 2025?

solution.concept: Use the share and the total of the same year
solution.explanation: Q's 2025 share is 28% of 50 lakh = 14 lakh units.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12.5 lakh uses Q's 2024 share (25%); 11.2 lakh uses the 2024 total (40 lakh); 10 lakh is Q's 2024 sales.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage did brand T's unit sales grow from 2024 to 2025?

solution.concept: Convert each year's share into units before comparing — the totals differ
solution.explanation: 2024: 10% of 40 lakh = 4 lakh. 2025: 12% of 50 lakh = 6 lakh. Growth = 2 ÷ 4 = 50%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% compares the shares (10% → 12%) and ignores the larger market; 2% is the change in percentage points.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Brand P's market share fell from 30% in 2024 to 26% in 2025. What happened to its unit sales?

solution.concept: A falling share of a growing market can still mean higher sales
solution.explanation: 2024: 30% of 40 lakh = 12 lakh. 2025: 26% of 50 lakh = 13 lakh. Sales rose by 1 lakh, which is 1 ÷ 12 = 8⅓%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 13⅓% fall is the relative fall in share (4 ÷ 30); 4% is the fall in percentage points; neither accounts for the market growing from 40 to 50 lakh.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage did the number of patients increase from March to April?

solution.concept: Percentage increase = rise ÷ earlier value × 100
solution.explanation: Patients rose from 440 to 484, an increase of 44, which is 44 ÷ 440 = 10%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9.09% uses April as the base; 44 is the rise in patients, not a percentage.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the ratio of the patients treated in January–March to those treated in April–June?

solution.concept: Sum each quarter, then reduce
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 : 4 is reversed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the average number of patients treated per month over the six months?

solution.concept: Average = total ÷ 6
solution.why_others_wrong: 540 divides the total by 5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The clinic charged a consultation fee of ₹300 per patient from January to March and ₹360 from April to June. Its fee income in April–June was what percentage more than in January–March?

solution.concept: Income = patients × fee; both factors change
solution.why_others_wrong: 25% counts only the rise in patients; 20% only the rise in fee; 45% adds the two percentages instead of multiplying the factors.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In which year were the firm's imports greater than its exports?

solution.concept: Compare the two lines year by year
solution.explanation: Only in 2023 is the imports line above the exports line: imports ₹150 crore against exports ₹135 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: In 2024 imports stayed at their 2023 level (₹150 crore), but exports rose to ₹180 crore.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the firm's total trade surplus (exports minus imports) over the five years taken together?

solution.concept: Net surplus = total exports − total imports (a deficit year counts as negative)
solution.explanation: Total exports = ₹795 crore and total imports = ₹706 crore, so the net surplus is ₹89 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹104 crore adds only the surplus years and ignores the ₹15 crore deficit in 2023; ₹119 crore adds that deficit instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage did the firm's total trade (exports + imports) grow from 2021 to 2025?

solution.concept: Growth of a sum is a weighted average of the growth rates, not a simple average
solution.explanation: Total trade was 120 + 100 = ₹220 crore in 2021 and 210 + 186 = ₹396 crore in 2025. Growth = 176 ÷ 220 = 80%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 75% is the growth of exports alone and 86% of imports alone; 80.5% is their simple average, which ignores that exports were the larger part in 2021.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many kilograms of apples spoiled?

solution.concept: First split 1,200 kg in the ratio 5 : 4 : 3
solution.explanation: Apples = 4/12 of 1,200 = 400 kg, and 5% of 400 kg = 20 kg spoiled.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40 kg is the spoiled mangoes and 30 kg the spoiled bananas.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the total amount the wholesaler paid for the fruit?

solution.concept: Cost = Σ (weight × price per kg) for each fruit
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹96,000 prices all 1,200 kg at the mango rate; ₹1,16,500 is the sales revenue.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How much did the wholesaler receive from selling mangoes?

solution.concept: Only the unspoiled weight is sold
solution.explanation: 8% of 500 kg = 40 kg spoiled, so 460 kg were sold at ₹100 per kg: ₹46,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹50,000 ignores spoilage; ₹36,800 uses the cost price per kg; ₹6,000 is the profit on mangoes.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the wholesaler's overall profit percentage on the whole deal?

solution.concept: Profit % = (total revenue − total cost) ÷ total cost × 100
solution.why_others_wrong: 25% ignores the spoiled fruit; 14.16% divides the profit by the revenue instead of the cost.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many tickets did Screen 1 sell on Saturday?

solution.concept: Tickets = seats × shows × occupancy
solution.explanation: Screen 1 offers 240 × 5 = 1,200 seats over the day, and 80% of them are filled: 960 tickets.
solution.why_others_wrong: 192 is the tickets for one show; 1,200 is the seats offered.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many seats did the multiplex offer in all on Saturday, counting every show?

solution.concept: Seats offered = seats per show × number of shows, summed over screens
solution.why_others_wrong: 690 is the seating capacity of the four screens for a single show each; 2,508 is the number of tickets actually sold.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was Screen 4's ticket revenue on Saturday?

solution.concept: Revenue = tickets sold × price
solution.explanation: Screen 4 offers 120 × 4 = 480 seats, 90% filled = 432 tickets. At ₹400 each, revenue = ₹1,72,800.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,92,000 assumes every seat was sold; ₹43,200 is the revenue from one show (108 tickets).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Taking all shows of all four screens together, what percentage of the seats offered on Saturday were filled?

solution.concept: An overall percentage is weighted by the seats offered, not a simple average of the four percentages
solution.why_others_wrong: 77.25% is the simple average of 80, 75, 64 and 90, which ignores that the screens offer different numbers of seats.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What were Anu's marks in Science?

solution.concept: Missing value = total − the known values
solution.explanation: Anu's total is 230, and Maths + English = 78 + 64 = 142. So Science = 230 − 142 = 88.
solution.why_others_wrong: 166 subtracts only the English marks (230 − 64).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What were the average Science marks of the five students?

solution.concept: Fill in the missing Science marks first, then average all five
solution.explanation: Missing Science marks: Anu 230 − 78 − 64 = 88 and Dev 210 − 66 − 70 = 74. Science total = 88 + 72 + 85 + 74 + 90 = 409, average 409 ÷ 5 = 81.8.
solution.why_others_wrong: 82.33 averages only the three Science marks shown; 102.25 divides 409 by 4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By how many marks is the average of Babu's three subject marks higher than the average of Dev's three subject marks?

solution.concept: Average of a row = row total ÷ 3; the missing cells do not change the given totals
solution.explanation: Babu's total is 238 and Dev's is 210, so the averages differ by (238 − 210) ÷ 3 = 28 ÷ 3 = 9⅓ marks.
solution.why_others_wrong: 28 is the difference in totals, not in averages.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What discount was allowed on the kettle?

solution.concept: Marked price = cost × (1 + markup); discount % is on the marked price
solution.explanation: Marked price = 800 × 1.25 = ₹1,000. It sold for ₹900, so the discount = 100 ÷ 1,000 = 10%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 11.11% divides the discount by the selling price; 12.5% is the kettle's profit percentage.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the markup percentage on the fan?

solution.concept: Work back: SP from profit %, then MP from discount %, then markup
solution.why_others_wrong: 32% adds 12% and 20%; 34.4% multiplies 1.12 by 1.2 instead of dividing by 0.8.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If the shop sells one unit of each of the five appliances, what is its overall profit as a percentage of the total cost?

solution.concept: Fill every missing value first; overall profit % = total profit ÷ total cost
solution.explanation: Selling prices: kettle ₹900, iron ₹1,190, fan ₹1,680, mixer 2,400 × 1.2 = ₹2,880, toaster 950 × 1.6 × 0.7 = ₹1,064. Iron's cost = 1,190 ÷ (1.4 × 0.85) = ₹1,000. Total cost = ₹6,650, total sales = ₹7,714, profit = ₹1,064, i.e. 16% of cost.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15.1% is the simple average of the five profit percentages; 13.79% divides the profit by total sales.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Profit percentage on an article bought for ₹80 and sold for ₹100
Quantity II: Discount percentage on an article marked at ₹500 and sold for ₹380

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Profit % is on cost price; discount % is on marked price
solution.explanation: Quantity I = 20 ÷ 80 × 100 = 25%. Quantity II = 120 ÷ 500 × 100 = 24%. So Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I < Quantity II' comes from taking the profit on the selling price (20 ÷ 100 = 20%).
solution.final_answer: Option D: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Area (cm²) of a square whose diagonal is 10 cm
Quantity II: Area (cm²) of a circle of radius 4 cm (take π = 3.14)

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Area of a square from its diagonal = d²/2
solution.explanation: Quantity I = 10² ÷ 2 = 50 cm². Quantity II = 3.14 × 16 = 50.24 cm². So Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' comes from taking the square's area as d² = 100.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The average of the first 15 multiples of 4
Quantity II: The average speed (km/h) of a car that goes from A to B at 30 km/h and returns from B to A at 34 km/h

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Average of an arithmetic sequence; average speed for equal distances = 2ab ÷ (a + b)
solution.explanation: Quantity I = (4 + 60) ÷ 2 = 32. Quantity II = 2 × 30 × 34 ÷ 64 = 31.875 km/h. So Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I = Quantity II or cannot be established' comes from averaging the speeds ((30 + 34) ÷ 2 = 32), which is wrong for equal distances.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Compound interest on ₹10,000 for 1 year at 20% per annum, compounded half-yearly
Quantity II: Simple interest on ₹7,200 for 3 years at 9.5% per annum

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Half-yearly compounding: half the rate, twice the periods
solution.explanation: Quantity I = 10,000 × (1.1² − 1) = 10,000 × 0.21 = ₹2,100. Quantity II = 7,200 × 9.5 × 3 ÷ 100 = ₹2,052. So Quantity I > Quantity II.
steps: I: 10% per half-year for 2 half-years ⇒ 1.21 ⇒ CI = 2,100
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I < Quantity II' comes from computing I as simple interest (₹2,000).
solution.final_answer: Option D: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Probability of getting a total of 9 when two fair dice are rolled
Quantity II: Probability that a card drawn at random from a pack of 52 is a king or a queen

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Classical probability; compare fractions by cross-multiplying
solution.explanation: Quantity I: totals of 9 are (3,6), (4,5), (5,4), (6,3), so 4/36 = 1/9 ≈ 0.111. Quantity II: 8/52 = 2/13 ≈ 0.154. So Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' comes from counting only kings for Quantity II (4/52 = 1/13, which is less than 1/9).
solution.final_answer: Option D: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The value of a, where a² = 49
Quantity II: The value of b, where b³ = −343

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: A square has two real roots (±); a cube has exactly one real root, with the same sign as the number
solution.explanation: a = 7 or −7. b³ = −343 has the single real root b = −7. If a = 7, a > b; if a = −7, a = b. So Quantity I ≥ Quantity II.
steps: II: b = −7 (only real cube root of −343)
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' forgets the root a = −7; 'Quantity I ≤ Quantity II' wrongly gives b two values.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Quantity I ≥ Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Each question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the two-digit number?
I. The sum of its digits is 9.
II. The number is 27 more than the number formed by reversing its digits.

options.text: Both statements I and II together are needed
Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Statements I and II together are not sufficient

solution.concept: Two unknown digits need two independent conditions
solution.explanation: Let the number be 10a + b. I gives a + b = 9 (18, 27, …, 90 all fit). II gives 9(a − b) = 27, so a − b = 3 (30, 41, 52, …, 96 all fit). Together, a = 6 and b = 3, so the number is 63. Both statements are needed.
steps: I alone: a + b = 9 — many numbers (18, 27, 36, …)
II alone: (10a + b) − (10b + a) = 9(a − b) = 27 ⇒ a − b = 3 — many numbers
Together: a + b = 9, a − b = 3 ⇒ a = 6, b = 3
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Statement I alone' ignores that every multiple of 9 from 18 to 90 has digit sum 9.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both statements I and II together are needed

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Each question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the area of the rectangular plot?
I. The perimeter of the plot is 34 m.
II. The diagonal of the plot is 13 m.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Both statements I and II together are needed
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Statements I and II together are not sufficient

solution.concept: Area = lw; (l + w)² = l² + w² + 2lw
solution.explanation: I gives l + w = 17, which allows many rectangles (for example 10 × 7 or 12 × 5, with different areas). II gives l² + w² = 169, which also allows many shapes. Together, 2lw = (l + w)² − (l² + w²) = 289 − 169 = 120, so the area lw = 60 m². Both are needed.
steps: I alone: l + w = 17 — area can be 70 (10 × 7), 60 (12 × 5), …
II alone: l² + w² = 169 — area not fixed
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Statement II alone' is tempting because 5-12-13 is a familiar triple, but other non-integer sides also have a 13 m diagonal (for example 2 m and √165 m).
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both statements I and II together are needed

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Each question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the cost price of the cooler?
I. The cooler was sold at a profit of 20%; had it been sold for ₹60 more, the profit would have been 25%.
II. The cooler's marked price is ₹1,800 and it was sold at a discount of 20%.

options.text: Both statements I and II together are needed
Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not

solution.concept: Statement I links two profit levels to a known rupee difference; II gives only the selling price
solution.explanation: I: the extra ₹60 moves the profit from 20% to 25%, so 5% of the cost = ₹60 and the cost = ₹1,200 — sufficient. II: the selling price is 1,800 × 0.8 = ₹1,440, but with no profit information the cost is unknown — not sufficient. (Together they agree: 1,200 × 1.2 = 1,440.)
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Both together' is chosen when II's selling price seems necessary, but I already fixes the cost.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements. Decide which statements are sufficient to answer it.
Question: In how many days can A alone finish a piece of work?
I. A and B together can finish it in 12 days.
II. B is 50% more efficient than A.
III. B alone can finish it in 20 days.

options.text: All three statements together are necessary
Any two of the three statements together are sufficient
Only statements I and III together are sufficient
Even all three statements together are not sufficient

solution.concept: Two unknowns (A's and B's rates); each statement is one equation
solution.explanation: I + II: A's rate a and B's rate 1.5a give 2.5a = 1/12, so A takes 30 days. I + III: a = 1/12 − 1/20 = 1/30, so 30 days. II + III: B's rate 1/20 = 1.5a gives a = 1/30, so 30 days. No single statement fixes A's time, but any two do.
steps: II alone: only a ratio of rates
III alone: says nothing about A
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Only I and III together' misses that II with either of the other two also works; 'all three' is more data than needed.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Any two of the three statements together are sufficient

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements. Decide which statements are sufficient to answer it.
Question: What is Ravi's monthly salary?
I. Ravi spends 30% of his salary on rent and 40% of the remainder on household expenses, and saves the rest, which is ₹8,400.
II. Ravi's salary is 25% more than Mohan's salary.
III. The salaries of Ravi and Sunil are in the ratio 5 : 4, and Sunil earns ₹4,000 less than Ravi.

options.text: Either statement I alone or statement III alone is sufficient
Statement I alone is sufficient, but III alone is not
Statement III alone is sufficient, but I alone is not
Statements II and III together are needed

solution.concept: Check each statement alone before combining; a statement with a new unknown (Mohan) adds nothing by itself
solution.explanation: I: savings = S × 0.7 × 0.6 = 0.42S = 8,400, so S = ₹20,000 — sufficient. II: S = 1.25 × Mohan's salary, which is unknown — not sufficient. III: S − 0.8S = 0.2S = 4,000, so S = ₹20,000 — sufficient. So either I alone or III alone answers the question.
steps: II: S = 1.25M with M unknown — not sufficient
Answer: either I alone or III alone
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I alone' and 'III alone' each name only one of the two sufficient statements; II and III are not both needed because III alone works.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Either statement I alone or statement III alone is sufficient
